topic: the relationship between mass and inertia

options.text: An object's resistance to a change in its motion
options.feedback: Correct -- inertia describes how much an object 'resists' speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.

options.text: The speed an object is traveling at
options.feedback: That describes velocity, not inertia.

options.text: The force of gravity on an object
options.feedback: That describes weight, a specific force, not the general concept of inertia.

options.text: The color of a moving object
options.feedback: Color has no bearing on the physics concept of inertia.

medium.text: Between a bowling ball and a tennis ball, which has more inertia?

options.text: The bowling ball, because it has more mass
options.feedback: Correct -- inertia is directly related to mass, so the more massive bowling ball has greater inertia.

options.text: The tennis ball, because it's smaller
options.feedback: Smaller size doesn't mean less inertia if we're comparing to a much more massive object -- mass, not size alone, determines inertia.

options.text: They have exactly the same inertia
options.feedback: Since their masses are very different, their inertia is different too, not equal.

options.text: Neither object has any inertia at all
options.feedback: All objects with mass have inertia -- both of these balls definitely have some.

hard.text: Why is it much harder to change the direction of a fully loaded truck than an empty shopping cart, even if both are moving at the same speed?

options.text: The truck has significantly more mass, giving it greater inertia and thus more resistance to any change in its motion
options.feedback: Correct -- greater mass means greater inertia, requiring more force to change the object's velocity or direction.

options.text: The truck is traveling faster than the shopping cart
options.feedback: The scenario specifies they're moving at the same speed, so speed isn't the differentiating factor here -- mass is.

options.text: The shopping cart has more inertia due to its wheels
options.feedback: Wheels don't determine inertia -- mass does, and the truck has far more mass than the cart.

options.text: There is no real difference in how hard it is to redirect them
options.feedback: There's a very real, significant difference due to the large disparity in mass between a loaded truck and an empty cart.

easy.hard: This property reflects how strongly an object resists any change to its current state of motion.
easy.medium: This is how much an object "wants" to keep doing what it's already doing.
easy.easy: This is how much something resists having its motion changed.

medium.hard: This resistance to motion change scales directly with how much matter (mass) the object contains.
medium.medium: More mass means more resistance to having its motion changed.
medium.easy: The heavier ball has more resistance to having its motion changed.

hard.hard: Since inertia scales directly with mass, and the truck vastly outweighs the cart, a proportionally much larger force is required to alter the truck's velocity or direction.
hard.medium: Since the truck weighs so much more, it takes a lot more force to change its direction compared to the much lighter cart.
hard.easy: Since the truck weighs so much more, it takes a lot more force to turn it compared to the light cart.

topic: the electromagnetic spectrum: infrared and ultraviolet

easy.text: Which type of electromagnetic wave is commonly associated with the heat you feel from a warm object?

options.text: Infrared radiation
options.feedback: Correct -- infrared radiation is closely associated with heat, which is why thermal cameras detect it.

options.text: Radio waves
options.feedback: Radio waves are used for broadcasting signals, not primarily associated with the sensation of heat.

options.text: Gamma rays
options.feedback: Gamma rays are extremely high-energy waves used in medical/industrial applications, not typically associated with everyday warmth sensation.

options.text: Visible light only
options.feedback: While visible light can carry some heat, infrared radiation is specifically and primarily associated with heat sensation.

medium.text: Why is ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun a concern for skin health?

options.text: UV radiation carries enough energy to damage skin cells and DNA, potentially causing sunburn or increasing cancer risk over time
options.feedback: Correct -- UV's higher energy (compared to visible light) makes it capable of causing this kind of biological damage.

options.text: UV radiation is actually harmless and has no effect on skin
options.feedback: UV radiation is a well-documented cause of sunburn and increased skin cancer risk with excessive exposure.

options.text: UV radiation only affects clothing, not skin directly
options.feedback: UV radiation directly affects exposed skin -- clothing can offer some protection, but skin protection is the primary health concern.

options.text: UV radiation is a type of sound wave, not related to skin health
options.feedback: UV radiation is an electromagnetic wave, not a sound wave, and it does have well-documented effects on skin.

hard.text: Infrared cameras can detect warm objects (like people) in complete darkness, without any visible light present. How is this possible?

options.text: Warm objects naturally emit infrared radiation due to their heat, and this radiation doesn't require visible light to exist or be detected
options.feedback: Correct -- infrared radiation is emitted by objects based on their temperature, independent of whether visible light is present in the environment.

options.text: Infrared cameras actually create their own visible light to illuminate the scene
options.feedback: Infrared cameras detect radiation the object itself emits due to heat -- they don't rely on producing visible light to see.

options.text: Warm objects don't actually emit any radiation of their own
options.feedback: Warm objects genuinely emit infrared radiation as a direct consequence of their thermal energy -- this is exactly the basis for infrared camera technology.

options.text: This technology only works in bright daylight, not darkness
options.feedback: Infrared cameras specifically excel in darkness, precisely because they detect heat-based infrared emission rather than relying on visible light.

easy.hard: This type of electromagnetic wave has a lower frequency than visible light and is closely tied to thermal energy.
easy.medium: This wave type is closely linked to the warmth given off by objects.
easy.easy: This wave type is closely linked to heat.

medium.hard: This wave type carries more energy than visible light, enough to potentially disrupt biological molecules like DNA.
medium.medium: This type of light carries enough energy to potentially harm living cells with too much exposure.
medium.easy: This type of light from the sun can burn skin with too much exposure.

hard.hard: All objects above absolute zero emit thermal (infrared) radiation proportional to their temperature, entirely independent of the presence or absence of visible light in the surrounding environment.
hard.medium: Any warm object naturally gives off this type of radiation just from having heat, whether or not there's any visible light around.
hard.easy: Warm objects naturally give off this radiation just from having heat, even in total darkness.

topic: the difference between AC and DC electric current

easy.text: What does 'DC' stand for in electrical current?

options.text: Direct current
options.feedback: Correct -- DC current flows steadily in one direction only.

options.text: Dual current
options.feedback: This isn't what the DC abbreviation actually stands for.

options.text: Digital current
options.feedback: This isn't what the DC abbreviation actually stands for.

options.text: Delayed current
options.feedback: This isn't what the DC abbreviation actually stands for.

medium.text: What is the key difference between AC (alternating current) and DC (direct current)?

options.text: AC periodically reverses direction, while DC flows steadily in one direction only
options.feedback: Correct -- this reversing behavior is exactly what "alternating" refers to in AC.

options.text: AC only works in batteries, while DC only works in wall outlets
options.feedback: This is actually backwards from typical usage -- batteries commonly provide DC, while wall outlets in most countries provide AC.

options.text: There is no real difference between AC and DC
options.feedback: These are genuinely distinct types of electrical current, differing in whether the flow direction changes over time.

options.text: AC only flows through water, while DC only flows through metal
options.feedback: Both AC and DC can flow through the same types of conductive materials -- the distinction isn't about the medium, but the current's directional behavior.

hard.text: Household electrical outlets typically supply AC power, while most portable electronics (like phones) run internally on DC power. Why does this mismatch require a power adapter/charger?

options.text: The adapter converts the alternating current from the outlet into the steady direct current that the device's internal circuitry actually needs
options.feedback: Correct -- this AC-to-DC conversion is a core function of most electronic chargers and power adapters.

options.text: The adapter simply makes the electricity travel faster
options.feedback: Speed of electrical flow isn't the adapter's main function -- converting between current types (AC to DC) is.

options.text: There is actually no real difference between the outlet's power and the device's needs
options.feedback: There IS a real, functional mismatch (AC vs DC) that specifically necessitates a conversion device.

options.text: The adapter's only job is to change the electricity's color
options.feedback: Electricity doesn't have a visible color in this sense -- the adapter's real job is converting between AC and DC current types.

easy.hard: This term describes current that flows consistently in a single direction over time.
easy.medium: This is current that flows in just one steady direction.
easy.easy: This is the type of current that flows in just one direction.

medium.hard: One current type periodically switches directions over time; the other maintains constant directional flow.
medium.medium: One type of current keeps switching back and forth; the other just flows one steady way.
medium.easy: One type keeps switching direction back and forth; the other just flows one way.

hard.hard: The adapter contains circuitry (a rectifier) that transforms the periodically reversing input current into the steady, one-directional output current the device's components require.
hard.medium: The charger has to change the back-and-forth power from the wall into the steady one-directional power the phone's insides actually need.
hard.easy: The charger changes the back-and-forth wall power into the steady power the phone's insides need.
